title: 🇪🇺 EU Arctic strategy: NGOs welcome EU ambition on cutting shipping's Arctic black carbon emissions
summary: The EU's new Arctic Strategy states it will support binding IMO regulations to limit shipping's black carbon emissions, a critical pollutant accelerating Arctic warming four times faster than the global average. Environmental groups welcome this ambition, advocating for mandatory "polar fuels" to replace current voluntary guidelines and a broader Arctic definition above 60°N. However, without immediate, enforceable measures at IMO PPR14 in January 2027, this remains merely rhetoric while black carbon continues to accelerate critical ice melt.
content:
October 20, 2026. Environmental groups have welcomed the European Union’s new Arctic Strategy, which states that the EU will support International Maritime Organization (IMO) regulations to limit the impact of black carbon emissions from ships in the Arctic. The strategy commits the EU to help move black carbon measures from voluntary guidelines to binding regulations and to advocate for a definition of wider Arctic waters above 60°N.

Polar fuels proposal

Dr Sian Prior, lead advisor to the Clean Arctic Alliance, said a mandatory regulation for “polar fuels” currently on the table at the IMO makes the EU’s ambition timely. The proposal, led by Denmark and supported by Greenland, and co-sponsored by Germany, France, and the Solomon Islands, would restrict ships to cleaner fuels while sailing in Arctic waters.

Prior said the EU’s call for a broad definition of Wider Arctic Waters reflects a clear understanding that black carbon from shipping travels further north and drives further ice melt and warming. Other Arctic and near-Arctic countries, she said, should now back the proposal when it is considered at the IMO’s Pollution Prevention and Response Committee in January 2027 (PPR14).

Calls on Arctic states

Andrew Dumbrille, special advisor to the Clean Arctic Alliance and co-director of Equal Routes, called on Canada to match the EU by backing a mandatory polar fuel measure covering the full Arctic. Black carbon from shipping is accelerating sea-ice melt in a region warming four times faster than the rest of the planet, he said.

Árni Finnsson, board chair of the Iceland Nature Conservation Association, said Iceland, which cooperates with the EU on climate policy, should support the polar fuels proposal at the IMO, in line with the Arctic policy Parliament adopted in 2022.

Karoline Andaur, CEO of WWF-Norway, called on the Norwegian government and other Arctic governments to support mandatory black carbon regulations at the IMO meeting in January 2027.

Other responses

Dr Kåre Press-Kristensen, senior advisor on air quality and climate at Green Global Future, said Greenland and Denmark had shown global climate leadership by leading the proposal, and that the strategy increases pressure on the IMO to act.

Sigurd Enge, senior advisor on shipping and Arctic issues at Bellona, welcomed the strategy’s position on black carbon. He said the strategy’s weaker signal on not buying Norwegian oil and gas from the Arctic was not helpful in reducing the environmental impact on vulnerable ecosystems.

About the Clean Arctic Alliance

The Clean Arctic Alliance is made up of 24 not-for-profit organisations that campaign to persuade governments to protect the Arctic, its wildlife, and its people. Members include Bellona, Greenpeace, WWF, Transport & Environment, and the Iceland Nature Conservation Association.
